task.problem_context: Two Sum precursor: dictionary mapping from number to index

observed_failure.description: The variable name used for a dictionary carried an existing set-related meaning for the learner and became an avoidable barrier to understanding the dictionary operation itself.
observed_failure.teacher_failure_condition: A tutor preserves or introduces a semantically misleading or learner-conflicting identifier even though the identifier is not part of the target concept and can be renamed without changing program behavior.

self_reported.text: The learner reported believing that the name 'seen' was associated with sets rather than dictionaries, which directly contributed to confusion about the operation.
After the dictionary was renamed to a descriptive identifier meaning number-to-index, the learner still reported that the name was confusing.
The learner reported that the neutral concrete identifier 'box' made the dictionary operation substantially clearer.
The learner explicitly identified the variable name itself as an important learning barrier and argued that arbitrary author naming should not become accidental concept difficulty.

observed.text: When asked to store number-to-index pairs in a dictionary named 'seen', the learner proposed checking the dictionary value instead of performing the intended assignment, then reported not understanding how the dictionary worked.
Renaming the same dictionary to a more descriptive number-to-index identifier did not resolve the learner's confusion.
After the mapping was represented with the neutral concrete identifier 'box' and a minimal key/value example, the learner correctly answered that retrieving the value stored under key 7 returns 1.

The learner then generalized the episode into a Study OS design requirement: author-selected variable language should not be allowed to become unnecessary difficulty when the identifier can be safely normalized.

derived.text: Study OS should test an identifier-normalization operation that replaces nonessential source identifiers with learner-intuitive names while preserving a reversible mapping to the original code.
Variable naming should be treated as a representation dimension that can create semantic interference independently of program semantics.

When a variable name is not itself part of the learning objective, failing to normalize a learner-conflicting identifier can count as a teacher/system failure if it adds avoidable decoding cost without preserving useful target difficulty.

system_should_be_penalized_when: an identifier creates learner confusion unrelated to the target concept
the identifier can be changed without altering program semantics or assessment validity
the tutor persists with the identifier despite direct learner confusion
system_should_recover_by: renaming the identifier to a lower-interference representation
preserving a reversible mapping to the source identifier
later reintroducing alternate/source identifiers after the concept is stable to build code-reading robustness

claims_supported: This canonical Study OS episode provides direct subject-level evidence that a variable name itself can become an avoidable learning barrier even when changing the identifier would not change program behavior.
For this learner, the identifier 'seen' carried a conflicting set-related interpretation and interfered with understanding the dictionary mapping operation.
A neutral concrete identifier was reported as clearer and was followed by a correct dictionary retrieval response.
The episode supports treating identifier choice as a measurable representation and teacher-quality variable.
not_yet_claimed: The episode does not establish that 'box' is the best identifier for all learners or contexts.
The episode does not establish a universal naming rule.
The immediate correct response does not establish durable dictionary mastery, transfer, or retention.

The episode does not by itself quantify how much of the performance change came from identifier normalization versus the accompanying simplification; however, the learner's explicit naming confusion remains direct evidence that the identifier itself was a barrier.
